title: Prevention, Scouting and IPM Decision Logic

content.overview: Integrated pest management is a decision framework for reducing pest and disease risk while preserving crop health, worker safety and control options. Prevention lowers introduction pressure; structured scouting converts observations into trends; diagnosis separates biological problems from environmental or nutritional lookalikes; thresholds or action criteria determine when intervention is justified; and follow-up determines whether the response actually worked.

vocabulary.definition: A repeatable inspection process used to detect pests, diseases, damage, and changing crop conditions.
Practices that reduce the introduction, survival, or spread of pests and pathogens through cleaning and handling controls.
The evidence-based process of identifying the most likely cause of a plant-health problem.
A prevention-first framework that combines monitoring and appropriate cultural, biological, physical, and chemical controls.

sections.title: Prevention comes before treatment
sections.body: Clean planting material, sanitation, controlled movement of tools and people, and appropriate environmental management can reduce the chance that a pest or pathogen becomes established. Preventive controls are usually easier to maintain than correcting a widespread problem later.

sections.title: Scouting creates usable evidence
sections.body: Routine scouting should be consistent enough to reveal changes over time. Record location, symptom pattern, pest presence, severity, and environmental context so observations can be compared rather than relying on memory or isolated photographs.

sections.title: Diagnosis should precede control choice
sections.body: Similar symptoms can have biological, environmental, nutritional, or mechanical causes. Before selecting a treatment, compare visible evidence with environmental conditions, root-zone information, crop history, and diagnostic observations so the response targets the actual problem.

sections.title: Controls should be proportionate and lawful
sections.body: A control should fit the identified problem, crop context, risk level, and applicable product restrictions. IPM favors the least disruptive effective response and continued monitoring rather than automatic escalation to the strongest available treatment.

workedExamples: Three adjacent plants develop stippling, while nearby sticky cards and leaf undersides reveal increasing mite-like arthropod counts. The spatial and direct-pest evidence is stronger than symptom appearance alone.
Leaf spots appear after a humidity event, but no pathogen signs are confirmed. Record the pattern and environment while keeping abiotic injury, spray damage and disease in the differential.
One bench shows repeated pest detections near an entry door. The pattern suggests a pathway or local source that prevention measures should address, not just repeated spot treatment.
A biological control is released, but scouting counts do not decline. IPM requires follow-up and reassessment rather than assuming the treatment succeeded because it was applied.
commonMistakes: Choosing a treatment before confirming the problem.
Scouting inconsistently so trends cannot be compared.
Recording only presence/absence without location and severity/count context.
Ignoring non-pest causes that mimic pest or disease injury.
Treating one control application as the end of the decision cycle.
Assuming a product is permitted or appropriate without checking the governing label/program.
content.practicalApplication: Run a repeatable scouting route using fixed zones and inspection points. Record pest/sign/symptom evidence, counts or severity, crop stage, environmental context and location. Build a short differential, identify the action criterion or escalation point, document the selected control pathway, and schedule follow-up evidence to verify effectiveness.
content.summary: IPM is a repeatable decision process: prevent problems, scout consistently, diagnose from evidence, choose proportionate controls, and verify outcomes. The quality of the diagnosis matters as much as the treatment choice.

blocks.title: IPM is a loop, not a spray decision
blocks.body: The core cycle is prevent → scout → identify/diagnose → decide → control → verify. Missing any step increases the chance of treating the wrong problem, responding too late or repeating an ineffective intervention.

blocks.title: Evidence hierarchy in scouting
rows: Bench edge, doorway, irrigation zone, clustered plants
Humidity event, wet canopy, heat stress
One leaf image with no plant/location history

items.title: Prevent
items.body: Control incoming plant material, sanitation and movement pathways.

items.title: Scout consistently
items.body: Use the same route, locations and observation method.

items.title: Describe before diagnosing
items.body: Record signs, symptoms, counts and spatial pattern.

items.title: Build a differential
items.body: Include pests, pathogens and non-biological lookalikes.

items.title: Apply the action criterion
items.body: Use the approved threshold/program rather than personal preference.

items.title: Select a lawful compatible control
items.body: Follow program, label and role requirements.

items.title: Verify
items.body: Repeat scouting and compare the post-control trend.

blocks.title: Spots after a humidity event
blocks.setting: Several plants develop leaf spots after two humid nights. No visible pest or confirmed pathogen sign is found yet.
blocks.prompt: What is the strongest next step?
options: Document distribution and context, collect diagnostic evidence, and keep abiotic and biological causes in the differential
Ignore the spots until the crop declines
blocks.answer: Document distribution and context, collect diagnostic evidence, and keep abiotic and biological causes in the differential.
blocks.feedback: Environmental history raises or lowers hypotheses but does not by itself identify the cause.

blocks.title: Create a scouting-to-decision record
blocks.instructions: Use a simulated room map with multiple plant-health observations.
prompts: Identify one discriminating observation/test for each.
Choose the next action under the supplied IPM program.
Define what follow-up evidence would show improvement.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: A control is only as good as the diagnosis and follow-up evidence behind it. IPM turns scouting data into repeatable decisions.
